clue.text: Begin, for instance, decapitating Prime Minister?

indicators.note: to decapitate is to cut off the head, so the first letter of the statesman's name is removed

parts.note: Benjamin Disraeli was a Victorian British Prime Minister

explanation.surface: A question about beheading a head of government, with Begin read as the verb 'start'.
explanation.walkthrough: Menachem Begin was Prime Minister of Israel, so 'Begin' is a name, not a verb; 'decapitating' removes the D from DISRAELI.
explanation.definitionFit: Menachem Begin was a national of the Jewish state, an example of one of its citizens.

clue.text: Cause provocation in popular celebrity, about fifty

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

indicators.note: the pieces for popular and celebrity are placed about, around, the letter for fifty

parts.note: fame means celebrity, renown
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A well-known star in their fifties stirs up trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: To inflame feelings is to arouse or provoke them, a synonym phrase.

clue.text: Chairman off the mark?

parts.note: a chairman or head of state who has left the starting line is setting off on the campaign trail for the top office

explanation.surface: A chairperson who has got something wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off the mark' looks like 'mistaken'; read it as a runner leaving the start, and the chairman as a president.
explanation.definitionFit: Running for the presidency means standing as a candidate to become chairman or head of state.

clue.text: Passing for performance in the theatre

explanation.surface: Something that goes on in place of a show at the playhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passing' is the passing of a law, not walking by; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill's passing into law is its enactment, and acting out a role on stage is also an enactment.

clue.text: Idly translated Latin poem

indicators.note: translated suggests the letters of idly are rendered into a different form, an anagram

explanation.surface: Someone lazily rendering a Latin poem into English.
explanation.definitionFit: An idyll is a short pastoral poem, the kind written by Theocritus.

clue.text: Gum containing lettuce, a source of energy

indicators.note: containing means the word for gum holds the lettuce inside it

parts.note: glue is a gum, an adhesive
cos is a variety of lettuce, romaine

explanation.surface: Chewing gum with lettuce in it as an energy snack.
explanation.definitionFit: This simple sugar is what the body's cells burn as fuel.

clue.text: Union supporter turning out nomograms

indicators.note: turning out signals that the letters of nomograms are reworked into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A trade union backer producing charts of figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' suggests a trade union, but it is a marriage: the supporter attends the groom.
explanation.definitionFit: At a wedding, a union of two people, the groom's attendants support him.

clue.text: Remove piano from front of club, say

indicators.note: remove tells us to take a letter away from the golf club word
from front of places the removed letter at the start of the club word

parts.note: a putter is a golf club
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: Instructions to shift a piano away from the entrance of a nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' is a golf club, not a nightclub; 'say' at the end is the definition, not 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: To utter words is to speak or say them.

clue.text: What would have gone with the toast to King William?

definitions.text: What would have gone with the toast to King William?

parts.words: What would have gone with the toast to King William?
parts.note: William III was William of Orange, so a breakfast spread named after his house would go with toast drunk or eaten in his honour

explanation.surface: Wondering what was drunk with a toast to the monarch William.
explanation.walkthrough: The toast is both the drink raised to King William and the bread at breakfast; his house was Orange.
explanation.definitionFit: A citrus preserve spread on toasted bread, sharing its name with William's royal house.

clue.text: Recruits forming untidy lines on either side of street

indicators.note: on either side of means the jumbled letters sit around the abbreviation for street
untidy suggests the letters of lines are messed up into a new order

explanation.surface: Army recruits lined up messily along both sides of a road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'untidy' shuffles LINES to ENLIS, which then goes 'on either side of' ST.
explanation.definitionFit: To recruit is to sign up, as one who joins the armed forces does.

clue.text: Mind game?

parts.note: a sport played only in the imagination, managing invented teams of real players

explanation.surface: A psychological manipulation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mind game' usually means manipulation; here it is a game played in the mind, with imaginary teams.
explanation.definitionFit: Players pick imaginary soccer squads whose scores follow real matches, a game of the imagination.

clue.text: Sailor dismissed roughly

parts.note: AB, able seaman, is a sailor
out means dismissed, as a batter is in cricket

explanation.surface: A seaman treated harshly and sent away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly' looks like an adverb of manner for 'dismissed' but is the definition, approximately.
explanation.definitionFit: About ten means roughly ten: approximately.

clue.text: Resort — resort merely obe used by soldiers

indicators.note: to re-sort is to sort again, so the letters of merely are put in a new order

parts.note: GIs are American soldiers

explanation.surface: A seaside town that troops fall back on.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'resort' is read as re-sort, the anagram indicator; LYME REGIS is a seaside town in Dorset, England.
explanation.definitionFit: This Dorset coastal town is a holiday destination.

clue.text: The effect of putting in a good word

definitions.text: The effect of putting in a good word

parts.words: The effect of putting in a good word
parts.note: putting in a good word usually means recommending someone; here it is replacing a harsh word with a mild one

explanation.surface: What happens when you speak up for someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting in a good word' means recommending; read literally it is substituting a nicer word.
explanation.definitionFit: A mild term substituted for a blunt one, like 'passed away' for died.

clue.text: Man people perhaps calumniate in middle of crisis?

indicators.note: in places the word for calumniate inside the letters taken from crisis
middle of picks the central pair of letters from crisis

parts.note: to calumniate is to slander, defame

explanation.surface: People who defame others at the heart of a crisis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the Isle of Man, between Britain and Ireland, so its people live on an island.
explanation.definitionFit: Residents of the Isle of Man live on an island, an example of the general word.

clue.text: Sound of machine American's used on garden soil

parts.note: a hum is the steady sound of a working machine
US means American

explanation.surface: An American's noisy machine working the garden soil.
explanation.definitionFit: Humus is the dark organic matter in fertile soil.

clue.text: Former Conservative in time must finally be the centre of attention

indicators.note: in places the former Conservative inside the word for time

parts.note: an hour is a period of time
old means former

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of must

explanation.surface: An ex-Tory politician wanting to be in the limelight.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold court is to preside over admirers, dominating a gathering.

clue.text: Way to consume small pudding

indicators.note: to consume means the word for way swallows the word for small

parts.note: ST, street, is a way
wee is Scottish for small

explanation.surface: A method for eating a little dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet is the British word for a dessert course.

clue.text: Article from France in a sense constitutes deception

indicators.note: in places the French article inside the word for a sense

parts.note: sight is one of the five senses
le is the French definite article

explanation.surface: A French newspaper article that in some sense is a deception.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a newspaper piece; it is the grammatical word 'le'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleight of hand is trickery, so sleight means cunning deception.

clue.text: Local authorities

parts.note: a local is a pub, so its authorities are the people who run the pub

explanation.surface: The council governing a town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local authorities' suggests councils; a 'local' is a British pub, and its bosses are the ones keeping it.
explanation.definitionFit: Publicans who run an inn are its masters, in charge of the bar.

clue.text: Title, unusually, to go from son to daughter-that's awkward

indicators.note: unusually signals that the letters of title are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: An aristocratic title passing from son to daughter, which is uncomfortable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go from son to daughter' puts the rearranged TITLE between S at the start and D at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Stilted speech is stiff and unnatural, which is awkward.

clue.text: Being sixteen, indisposed to go to church

indicators.note: indisposed means unwell, out of sorts, so the letters of sixteen are rearranged

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A sick sixteen-year-old going to church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being' starts the sentence as a verb but is the noun, life.
explanation.definitionFit: Existence is the state of being alive or real.

clue.text: Nominal number of commandments is about right

indicators.note: is about places the number around the word for right

parts.note: there are ten commandments
OK means all right

explanation.surface: Whether the count of commandments being ten is correct.
explanation.definitionFit: A token payment is a nominal one, small and symbolic.

clue.text: Log books kept by eastern head of state

indicators.note: kept by means the books are held inside the other pieces

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, was the British head of state
NT is the New Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: Records kept by an eastern ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Log' is the verb, to record; ER (Queen Elizabeth) is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: To log data is to record it, as one does when entering it into a system.

clue.text: Exotic mammal, one with fur

parts.note: a fur is a coat
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An unusual animal with fur.
explanation.definitionFit: The coati is a raccoon-like animal of South America.

clue.text: Eatery providing classic cuisine?

parts.note: classic refers to the classical world of ancient Athens, so the cuisine comes from that country

explanation.surface: A restaurant offering traditional dishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classic' means traditional on the surface, but Classics are ancient Greek and Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: A place serving moussaka and souvlaki, food of the classical land.

indicators.note: about means the word read goes around the trimmed tyre
lacking means a letter is missing from tyre
ultimately picks the last letter of safety

explanation.surface: Reading about a tyre without safety, which is cheaper in the end.
